note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in MD.json, gathered 2026-10-05. "review" holds research notes for a human check; "issues" lists open questions.

byways.name: Historic National Road
byways.designation: Maryland Scenic Byway; All-American Road (National Road)
byways.where: MD 144, MD 27, US 40 Alt, US 40, I-68, I-70; Baltimore to the Pennsylvania line near Grantsville

facts.fact: The Maryland route runs 173 miles from Baltimore to Grantsville at the state line.
The La Vale Toll Gate House is Maryland's only remaining National Road toll gate house.
The Casselman River Bridge near Grantsville is a single-span stone arch built for the National Road in 1813.

byways.name: Chesapeake and Ohio Canal
byways.where: MD 189, MD 190, MD 28, MD 34, MD 65, MD 63, MD 56, MD 144, US 40, I-70 and others; Washington, D.C. to Cumberland, with a loop through Paw Paw, W.Va.

facts.fact: The byway runs 236 miles from Washington, D.C. to Cumberland.
The Conococheague Aqueduct is near Lockhouse 44 in Williamsport.
The Paw Paw Tunnel cuts through more than 3,000 feet of rock between Hancock and Cumberland.
Great Falls of the Potomac made the river unnavigable and prompted the canal.

byways.name: Journey Through Hallowed Ground
byways.designation: Maryland Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 15, US 340, MD 355, MD 77, MD 17; Point of Rocks to Emmitsburg (Maryland section)

facts.fact: The Maryland section runs 57 miles from Point of Rocks to Emmitsburg.
The national byway runs from Monticello, Virginia, to Gettysburg, Pennsylvania; the Maryland section was formerly the Catoctin Mountain Scenic Byway.
Catoctin Furnace made shells for the Battle of Yorktown.
Cunningham Falls State Park has a 78-foot waterfall dropping into a rocky gorge.

byways.review: Formerly the Catoctin Mountain Scenic Byway. Multi-state national byway; MDOT SHA layer draws only the Maryland section.

byways.name: Antietam Campaign
byways.where: MD 107, MD 109, MD 28, MD 355, MD 85, MD 80, US 40 Alt, MD 17, MD 67, MD 34; White's Ferry to Sharpsburg

facts.fact: The route runs 126 miles from White's Ferry to Sharpsburg.
Union troops gathered at Poolesville in 1861 before crossing for the Battle of Ball's Bluff.
Tolson's Chapel in Sharpsburg is a log-and-frame church built by an African American congregation in 1866.

byways.name: Baltimore's Historic Charles Street
byways.designation: Maryland Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway
byways.where: Charles Street (MD 139) and St. Paul Street; Inner Harbor to Lutherville

facts.fact: Charles Street runs about 12 miles from the Inner Harbor north to Lutherville.
The Washington Monument at Mount Vernon Place is 178 feet tall with a 16-foot statue of Washington on top.
Charles Village was developed in the late 19th century as one of Baltimore's first suburban neighborhoods.

byways.name: Star-Spangled Banner
byways.where: MD 4, MD 2, MD 765, MD 231, MD 381, MD 382, US 301, MD 202 and others; Hollywood (St. Mary's County) to Edgemere, with Baltimore harbor streets

facts.fact: The byway runs 106 miles from Hollywood to Edgemere.
Sotterley is a 300-year-old Tidewater plantation house overlooking the Patuxent River.
The British bombarded Fort McHenry through the night with Congreve rockets and mortar shells; the flag that flew at dawn measured 42 by 30 feet.

byways.review: MDOT SHA layer includes Baltimore harbor streets (Fort Ave, Lawrence St, Light St, Eastern Ave) that look like the former National Historic Seaport loop.

byways.name: Booth's Escape
byways.where: MD 5, Brandywine Road, Poplar Hill Road, MD 6, US 301; Washington, D.C. to Popes Creek and the Potomac crossing

facts.fact: The route runs 66 miles following John Wilkes Booth's escape after he shot Lincoln on April 14, 1865.
The Surratt House Museum in Clinton was a tavern where Booth and Herold stopped for supplies.
Dr. Samuel Mudd treated Booth's broken leg on April 15, 1865, at his house off Poplar Hill Road.

byways.review: Visit Maryland's index page titles it 'John Wilkes Booth: Chasing Lincoln's Assassin'; the GIS TOURISM_URL /scenic-byways/booths-escape also loads.

byways.name: Religious Freedom
byways.designation: Maryland Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway
byways.where: MD 6, MD 425, MD 224, MD 234, MD 238, MD 243, MD 5, MD 249; Port Tobacco to Point Lookout, Charles and St. Mary's counties

facts.fact: The byway runs from Port Tobacco to Point Lookout through Charles and St. Mary's counties.
St. Ignatius Church was established by the Jesuits in 1641 and is the oldest continuously serving Catholic parish in the nation.
Historic St. Mary's City was Maryland's first capital, from 1634 to 1695.

byways.review: GIS BYWAY_NAME is misspelled 'Religous Freedom Tour'. Visit Maryland calls it Religious Freedom (URL slug religious-freedom-tour).

byways.name: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad
byways.where: MD 341, MD 16, MD 335, MD 14, MD 331, MD 313, MD 287; Cambridge to Goldsboro, Dorchester and Caroline counties

facts.fact: The byway runs 125 miles from Cambridge to Goldsboro.
Around 1835 at the Bucktown Village Store Tubman tried to help an enslaved man avoid capture and was nearly killed.
The Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge landscape is largely unchanged since Tubman's time.

byways.name: Mountain Maryland
byways.where: I-68, MD 42, US 219, MD 135, MD 495, MD 36; Keysers Ridge to Cumberland, Garrett and Allegany counties

facts.fact: The byway runs 193 miles from Keysers Ridge to Cumberland.
Swallow Falls State Park has Maryland's tallest free-falling waterfall.
At Cranesville Subarctic Swamp a boardwalk leads into a bog where carnivorous plants grow.
Deep Creek Lake, with rentals at McHenry, is on the route.
The byway's segments in the MDOT SHA layer lie in Garrett and Allegany counties (route IDs prefixed 11 and 01).

byways.name: Old Main Streets
byways.where: MD 140, MD 832, MD 84, MD 31, MD 27, MD 26, MD 75, MD 77; loop from Emmitsburg to Thurmont, Frederick and Carroll counties

facts.fact: Emmitsburg's Main Street is lined with buildings from the late 1700s.
The National Shrine of St. Elizabeth Ann Seton honors the first American-born saint.
The byway passes three covered bridges near Thurmont: Loy's Station, Roddy Road and Utica Mills.

byways.name: Falls Road
byways.where: MD 25 (Falls Road) and MD 130 (Greenspring Valley Road); Baltimore City to northern Baltimore County

facts.fact: Jones Falls valley mills sent goods to the city on the Falls Road Turnpike; many survive as shops, galleries and homes.
Bare Hills was a free Black community from the 1800s, named for its mining operations.
The byway follows MD 25 Falls Road and MD 130 Greenspring Valley Road.

byways.name: Horses and Hounds
byways.where: Shawan Road, MD 128, MD 138, MD 146, Dulaney Valley Road, Long Green Pike and others; loop north of Towson, Baltimore and Harford counties

facts.fact: Sagamore Farm, a 425-acre thoroughbred farm, was home to Native Dancer, who won 21 of 22 races.
Ladew Topiary Gardens has 22 acres of sculpted shrubbery.
The Maryland Hunt Cup steeplechase is run in Worthington Valley, which the byway crosses on Tufton Avenue.

byways.name: Lower Susquehanna
byways.where: MD 155, MD 161, US 1, MD 222; Havre de Grace to Perryville, Harford and Cecil counties

facts.fact: The byway runs 33 miles between Havre de Grace and Perryville.
Hawks, great blue herons and bald eagles can be seen near Conowingo Dam.
The Havre de Grace Decoy Museum shows hand-carved waterfowl decoys.
Rodgers Tavern in Perryville dates to the Revolutionary War and was visited by Washington and Lafayette.

byways.name: Mason and Dixon
byways.where: MD 97, MD 496, MD 25, MD 45, MD 23, MD 136, MD 24, US 1, MD 273; Westminster to Appleton at the Delaware line

facts.fact: Union Mills Homestead was built in 1797 and ran as a grist mill; Union and Confederate soldiers stopped there on the way to Gettysburg.
The byway runs from Westminster to Appleton.
The byway runs a short distance south of the Mason-Dixon line and crosses the Susquehanna on Conowingo Dam before ending at the Delaware border.
Fair Hill hosts turf-course horse racing on Memorial Day weekend.

byways.name: Chesapeake Country
byways.designation: Maryland Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway (Chesapeake City to Stevensville section)
byways.where: MD 213, MD 18, US 50, MD 33, MD 333, MD 16, MD 349, MD 352, US 13, MD 413 and others; Chesapeake City to Crisfield

facts.fact: The byway runs 419 miles from Chesapeake City to Crisfield.
The Wye Grist Mill is described as the oldest continuously working water-powered grist mill in the country.
Smith Island is Maryland's only inhabited island reachable only by boat.
The Lower Eastern Shore section was originally the western part of the Blue Crab Scenic Byway; the national byway covers Stevensville to Chesapeake City.

byways.review: Catalog line (84 mi) is only the national section; the state byway now runs about 419 miles and absorbed the western half of the former Blue Crab Scenic Byway. The MDOT SHA layer value 'Chesapeake Country' draws the full line.

byways.name: Roots and Tides
byways.where: MD 2, MD 253, MD 468, MD 256, MD 423, MD 261; Annapolis to Huntingtown, Anne Arundel and Calvert counties

facts.fact: The byway runs 47 miles from Annapolis to Huntingtown.
Historic London Town in Edgewater is a 23-acre site where archaeologists have found 18th-century artifacts.
The Smithsonian Environmental Research Center covers 2,800 acres of forest, farmland, wetlands and tidal marsh.

byways.name: Cape to Cape
byways.where: MD 528, US 50, MD 611, MD 376, MD 818, US 113, MD 12, MD 365; Ocean City to the Virginia line below Snow Hill, Worcester County

facts.fact: Maryland's section runs 79 miles from Ocean City to Stockton; the full route runs 200 miles from Cape May, N.J., to Cape Henry, Va.
Assateague's wild ponies live in bands of two to twelve.
The Pocomoke River has one of the northernmost stands of bald cypress.
Cape to Cape was originally the eastern part of the Blue Crab Scenic Byway.

byways.review: Not in the catalog as its own road; it is the eastern half of catalog entry blue-crab-scenic-byway-60591. Draw from MDOT SHA layer, BYWAY_NAME = 'Cape to Cape'.

issues: Catalog road national-historic-seaport-2270 is no longer one of the 18 current byways; its Inner Harbor streets seem to be carried in the Star-Spangled Banner line of the GIS layer. Hide it or fold it in.

Catalog road blue-crab-scenic-byway-60591 is superseded: its western half is now the Lower Eastern Shore section of Chesapeake Country and its eastern half is Cape to Cape. Hide it and draw Cape to Cape from the GIS layer (BYWAY_NAME = 'Cape to Cape').

Catalog chesapeake-country-scenic-byway-2261 (84 mapped miles) covers only the national section; the state byway is about 419 miles to Crisfield. Consider redrawing from the GIS layer value 'Chesapeake Country'.

Mileages on Visit Maryland pages differ from catalog mapped miles for several byways (Antietam Campaign 126 vs 80, Star-Spangled Banner 106 vs 137, Horses and Hounds 70 vs 121, Mason and Dixon 143 vs 110). The catalog lines may be older alignments; the GIS layer is current.

Visit Maryland pages return 403 to curl; they were checked with a browser-style fetch. Booth's Escape has two working slugs (booths-escape in the GIS layer, john-wilkes-booth-chasing-lincolns-assassin on the index page).
www.chesapeakebyway.org (listed on Wikipedia as the Chesapeake Country official site) now redirects to an unrelated domain; not used.
Visit Maryland gives Old Main Streets endpoints as Emmitsburg to Thurmont and Mason and Dixon as Westminster to Appleton, while Wikipedia starts Mason and Dixon in Emmitsburg.
Left out of the chapter: Former Maryland Scenic Byways (no longer listed): National Historic Seaport, Blue Crab Scenic Byway
